title: Hierarchical Reasoning Model
relevance_reason: Founding recursive-reasoning model: two weight-reused Transformer modules iterated at two timescales, with deep supervision and ACT halting over segments.
one_sentence: HRM couples a slow high-level and a fast low-level Transformer module (N cycles of T steps), trains with a one-step gradient plus deep supervision and Q-learned halting, and reports 40.3% ARC-AGI-1, 55.0% Sudoku-Extreme, 74.5% Maze-Hard at 27M parameters from ~1000 examples.
key_contributions: Two-module nested recurrence (L updates every step with H state and input added; H updates once per T L-steps) giving effective depth N*T per forward pass ('hierarchical convergence').
One-step (last-state) gradient justified via DEQ/IFT Neumann truncation, plus deep supervision over M segments with detached state and Q-learning ACT halting (halt/continue head).
Small-sample results on ARC-AGI-1/2, Sudoku-Extreme (1000 train) and Maze-Hard 30x30 (1000 train) versus CoT LLMs and a same-size Transformer 'Direct pred' baseline.

setup.model_sizes: ~27M parameters; H and L modules are encoder-only Transformer blocks with identical architecture (Llama-style: RoPE, GLU, RMSNorm, Post-Norm). Per-module layer count not stated in main text.
setup.train_tokens_or_data: ~1000 examples per task: Sudoku-Extreme 1000 train (Sudoku-Extreme-Full 3,831,994 for analysis), Maze-Hard 1000 train/1000 test, ARC-AGI-1 960 and ARC-AGI-2 1120 training examples per Fig. 1; ARC training also includes evaluation-set demonstration pairs and test inputs, heavily augmented.
setup.loops_train: N high-level cycles x T low-level steps per segment (pseudocode default N=2, T=2); up to Mmax segments with deep supervision; Mmax in {2,4,8} in Fig. 5.
setup.loops_test: Increase Mmax at inference (e.g. train Mmax=8, test Mmax=16 on Sudoku-Extreme-Full).
setup.baselines: o3-mini-high, Claude 3.7 8K, DeepSeek R1 (API / ARC leaderboard), 'Direct pred' Transformer of same size and training setup, recurrent Transformer (Fig. 2).
setup.benchmarks: ARC-AGI-1, ARC-AGI-2 (pass@2 via 1000-augmentation voting), Sudoku-Extreme (exact match, single pass), Maze-Hard 30x30 (optimal path, single pass).

claims.claim: HRM at 27M params trained from scratch on ~1000 ARC examples reaches 40.3% on ARC-AGI-1, above o3-mini-high and Claude 3.7 8K.
claims.regime: unmatched (CoT LLM scores taken from leaderboard; different data, scale and protocol)
claims.evidence_quote: with only 27M parameters and a 30x30 grid context (900 tokens), achieves a performance of 40.3%, which substantially surpasses leading CoT-based models like o3-mini-high (34.5%) and Claude 3.7 8K context (21.2%)

claims.claim: Against a same-size Transformer trained with the identical setup ('Direct pred'), swapping in HRM's hierarchy plus ACT more than doubles ARC-AGI-1 performance.
claims.regime: iso_param, iso_data (same training setup, same size)
claims.evidence_quote: By substituting the Transformer architecture with HRM's hierarchical framework and implementing ACT, we achieve more than a twofold performance improvement.

claims.claim: On Sudoku-Extreme-Full, increasing width does not help while depth helps; standard (and recurrent) Transformers saturate with depth while HRM keeps improving.
claims.regime: iso_effective_depth (x-axis is layers computed), analysis on full 3.8M-example data
claims.evidence_quote: increasing a Transformer's width yields no performance gain, while increasing depth is critical. Right: Standard architectures saturates, failing to benefit from increased depth.

claims.claim: One-step gradient approximation trains with O(1) memory in recurrence steps instead of BPTT's O(T).
claims.evidence_quote: This design maintains a constant memory footprint (O(1) compared to BPTT's O(T ) for T timesteps) throughout the backpropagation process, making it scalable and more biologically plausible.

claims.claim: ACT halting reaches accuracy comparable to fixed-M compute while using substantially fewer segments on average; raising Mmax at inference improves Sudoku accuracy without retraining, but gives minimal gains on ARC.
claims.evidence_quote: On the other hand, we find that extra computational resources yield minimal gains in ARC-AGI challenge, as solutions generally require only a few transformations.

claims.claim: The high-level state has higher participation ratio (dimensionality) than the low-level state after training, absent in an untrained net; authors stress this is correlational.
claims.evidence_quote: We emphasize, however, that this evidence is correlational. While a causal link could be tested via intervention (e.g., by constraining the H-module's dimensionality), such methods are difficult to interpret in deep learning

limitations: Brain-correspondence evidence is correlational; extra inference compute gives minimal ARC gains; module/merging design (element-wise addition) left simple; the underlying algorithm learned is not characterized. No per-component ablation of hierarchy vs. one-step gradient vs. deep supervision vs. ACT in the paper (later papers do this).
survey_notes: Anchor of the 'recursive reasoning models' subsection. Template instance: 2 modules (H,L) with separate weights (each tied across its own steps), inner recursion T L-steps per H-step, N H-cycles per segment, outer recursion = deep-supervision segments (up to Mmax) with detached state; one-step gradient (only last L and H step get gradients); Q-learning halting; ARC uses puzzle-ID embedding, train-on-eval-demonstrations, 1000-augmentation majority vote, pass@2. Protocol caveat: ARC numbers are transductive (eval demonstrations in training) and depend on 1000-sample voting; 2512.11847 shows similar voting adds ~11pp for TRM and puzzle-ID removal zeroes accuracy. The 'Direct pred' baseline is iso-param but not iso-effective-depth. 2609.39967 finds the explicit hierarchy unnecessary; TRM (2510.04871, sibling group) and 2605.17811 also question the two-module split. Fig. 1 Sudoku/Maze numbers (55.0/74.5) are used as the HRM reference by 2604.13521 and others.

title: HRM-Text: Efficient Pretraining Beyond Scaling
relevance_reason: Brings the HRM two-timescale recurrent architecture to 1B-scale language-model pretraining from scratch, with training-FLOP-matched comparisons to looped Transformers, RINS and TRM.
one_sentence: HRM-Text pretrains a 1B HRM (2 H-cycles x 3 L-steps, MagicNorm, truncated backprop warmed from 2 to 5 steps) on 40B unique instruction-response tokens with response-only loss and PrefixLM masks, beating FLOP-matched Transformers, looped Transformers, RINS and TRM.
key_contributions: MagicNorm (PreNorm blocks inside each module, a norm at module exit) and warmup deep credit assignment (backward horizon K=2 linearly to K=5) to stabilize HRM recurrence for language.

Task-completion pretraining on instruction-response pairs with response-only NLL and PrefixLM attention; incremental ablation shows each of objective, PrefixLM and HRM architecture adds accuracy under matched FLOPs.
Training-FLOP-matched comparison of HRM 1B vs Transformer 1B/3B, Looped Transformer, RINS and TRM; logit-lens and block-difference analyses of effective depth.

setup.model_sizes: HRM-Text 1B (each module 16 layers, hidden 1536, head size 128); also 0.6B; Transformer baselines 1B and 3B (deep/wide).
setup.train_tokens_or_data: 40B unique tokens sampled from ~176.5B-token open instruction corpus; 60B tokens total training; 46 hours on two 8xH100 nodes.
setup.loops_train: H2L3: 2 H cycles each with 3 L steps (8 module steps, counted as 4 recursions of the full core); backward horizon warmed from 2 to 5 steps.
setup.loops_test: Same fixed schedule; no ACT used.
setup.baselines: Transformer 1B, Transformer 3B deep/wide, Looped Transformer 1B, RINS 1B, TRM 1B/0.6B (FLOP-matched); Llama3.2 3B, Gemma3 4B, Qwen3.5 2B, Olmo3 7B, Huginn 3.5B, Ouro 1.4B (unmatched public checkpoints).
setup.benchmarks: MMLU, ARC-C, HellaSwag, WinoGrande, BoolQ, DROP, GSM8K, MATH.

claims.claim: Under matched training FLOPs, HRM 1B outperforms Transformer 1B, Transformer 3B (deep and wide), Looped Transformer 1B and RINS 1B on all eight reported benchmarks.
claims.regime: iso_train_flop (Transformer 1B sees 0.17T tokens vs 0.06T for HRM; 3B and recurrent baselines see 0.06T, so also iso_data for those)
claims.evidence_quote: We test this by comparing standard Transformers, larger matched-FLOPs Transformers, Looped Transformers 33 , RINS 34 , and HRM under matched training compute.

claims.claim: Looped Transformers and RINS beat same-size Transformers, but their advantage over a larger FLOP-matched Transformer is inconsistent.
claims.evidence_quote: Looped Transformers and RINS generally outperform Transformer models of the same size, showing that recurrent or looped computation is an effective architectural direction. When compared with a larger Transformer under a matched training-FLOPs budget, however, their advantage is less consistent.

claims.claim: TRM (shared H/L weights) trained at 1B with reduced recursions is unstable; at 0.6B with the same H2L3 recursion it roughly matches HRM 0.6B but needs about 2x the training FLOPs.
claims.evidence_quote: HRM maintains stable training dynamics across all scales, whereas TRM suffers from severe instability at the 1B parameter scale.

claims.claim: Response-only (task-completion) loss, PrefixLM masking and the HRM architecture each add accuracy in an incremental FLOP-matched ablation.
claims.evidence_quote: As shown in Table 3, the task-completion objective, PrefixLM training, and the HRM architecture each significantly contribute to overall performance.

claims.claim: Against public 2-7B open models trained on far more tokens, HRM-Text 1B is competitive with 96-432x less estimated training compute; this is an unmatched comparison (different data, instruction-only corpus).
claims.evidence_quote: HRM-Text reaches this performance range with 96-432× less estimated training compute and roughly 100-900× fewer training tokens than the compared open baselines.

claims.claim: Full BPTT through the HRM unroll produces rare large gradient spikes; the used truncation is the deepest setting that remains stable.
claims.evidence_quote: The truncation setting used in our experiments is the closest setting to full BPTT that remains stable during training, as illustrated in Figure 6a and Figure 7.

numbers.quote: The core processing sequence consists of two high-level cycles. Each cycle executes three fast L module updates followed by a single slow H module update.

numbers.what: Backward horizon warmup
numbers.quote: During early pretraining, we compute gradients through only the last two recurrent steps (K = 2), then linearly warm up

numbers.what: Module configuration
numbers.quote: Each module is a transformer comprising 16 layers, with a hidden size of 1536 and a head size of 128.

limitations: Scaling shown only up to 1B HRM / 3B Transformer; no ACT, so inference cost is higher than a single-pass Transformer; training data are instruction/task-formatted (incl. Sudoku-Extreme, GSM-style math), so comparisons to raw-text-pretrained public checkpoints confound architecture with objective and data; DROP shows significant contamination at n=13.
survey_notes: Main bridge from recursive-reasoning puzzles to language modeling. Template: 2 modules (separate weights), N=2 H cycles x T=3 L steps, no deep supervision across segments mentioned, no halting, truncated BPTT with growing horizon (departs from HRM's 1-step gradient), MagicNorm. Strongest evidence is Table 1 (iso-train-FLOP incl. a 3B deep Transformer at equal tokens); note iso-inference-FLOP is NOT matched (HRM does 4 core recursions per token). The Table 3 ablation shows objective+PrefixLM account for a large share of gains (Transformer 1B MMLU 40.55 -> 53.15 from objective/mask alone; HRM adds 53.15 -> 60.73). Contradiction: TRM paper argues single shared network is better on puzzles; HRM-Text finds TRM unstable at 1B and weaker per FLOP. Mimir v1 (2608.13517) builds on HRM-Text and claims to beat it. 2604.14442 (HRM-LM) also reports hierarchical shared-weight recurrence in LM context.

title: Continuous Thought Machines
relevance_reason: Weight-tied recurrent model unrolled over a decoupled internal 'tick' dimension with certainty-based adaptive compute; not a looped Transformer stack but a latent-iteration reasoner evaluated on mazes and parity.
one_sentence: CTM iterates a shared U-Net synapse MLP plus per-neuron private MLPs over internal ticks, uses neuron-pair synchronization as its representation, and trains on min-loss and max-certainty ticks, solving 39x39 mazes without positional encodings and showing certainty-based early stopping.
key_contributions: Internal tick dimension decoupled from data; neuron-level models with private weights process a sliding history of pre-activations; synchronization matrix of post-activation histories drives outputs and attention queries.
Loss over two dynamically selected ticks (minimum loss and maximum certainty) which yields native adaptive compute without a halting module.

Experiments on 39x39 maze route prediction without positional embeddings (generalizing to 99x99 by re-application), ImageNet-1K, cumulative parity, sorting, Q&A MNIST and RL; parameter-matched ablation of NLMs and synchronization.

setup.model_sizes: Maze CTM 31,998,330 parameters; ablation models ~9M; LSTM baselines 42M-109M.
setup.loops_train: 75 internal ticks for mazes (LSTMs also at 50); 50 ticks ImageNet; parity up to 100 ticks.
setup.loops_test: Same ticks; certainty threshold allows halting early; mazes larger than training solved by repeated re-application.
setup.baselines: LSTMs (1-3 layers, 50/75 ticks), feed-forward; parameter-matched CTM variants without NLMs or without synchronization; LSTM+synch.
setup.benchmarks: 2D mazes 39x39 (and 99x99 generalization), ImageNet-1K, parity-64, CIFAR-10/100, sorting, Q&A MNIST, CartPole/Acrobot/MiniGrid.

claims.claim: On 39x39 maze route prediction (sequence-of-actions output, no positional embeddings), CTM outperforms LSTM and feed-forward baselines and generalizes to 99x99 mazes by re-application.
claims.regime: unmatched (LSTM baselines have more parameters; ticks matched at 75)
claims.evidence_quote: The CTM significantly outperforms the baselines in solving these mazes, demonstrating superior trainability and generalization to longer paths (Figure 4).

claims.claim: Adaptive computation emerges from the two-tick loss: with a 0.8 certainty threshold most ImageNet instances could halt before 10 of 50 ticks.
claims.evidence_quote: setting a certainty threshold of 0.8 (Figure 5a) means that a user could halt compute for the majority of instances after fewer than 10 of 50 internal ticks.

claims.claim: On cumulative parity, CTM accuracy improves with internal ticks and beats parameter-matched LSTMs.
claims.evidence_quote: The CTM's accuracy improves with more internal ticks, significantly outperforming parametermatched LSTMs, which struggled with stability and performance (Figure 6b).

claims.claim: Parameter-matched ablations on 15x15 mazes show both neuron-level models and synchronization are needed (CTM 66% solve rate; variants below 50%).
claims.evidence_quote: We find that the two augmented variants of the CTM and the LSTM with synchronization were unable to achieve a solve rate above 50%. The standard CTM, on the other hand, achieves a solve rate of 66% and a per-step accuracy of 95%.

numbers.what: ImageNet-1K accuracy with 50 ticks and ResNet-152 backbone
numbers.quote: internal ticks and a ResNet-152 backbone: 72.47% top-1, 89.89% top-5 on uncropped data).

numbers.what: Maze CTM parameter count
numbers.quote: This resulted in a model with 31,998,330 parameters.

numbers.what: Maze ablation (15x15, ~9M params) CTM solve rate and per-step accuracy
numbers.quote: The standard CTM, on the other hand, achieves a solve rate of 66% and a per-step accuracy of 95%.

numbers.what: Internal ticks for maze CTM and LSTM
numbers.quote: For the CTMs and LSTM baselines, we used 75 internal ticks, but LSTM stability issues meant that using 50 internal ticks yielded superior performance, so we report these too.

limitations: Internal sequence lengthens training; NLMs add parameters; experiments are preliminary and favor breadth over depth of comparison; not aimed at SOTA.
venue: 39th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2025).
survey_notes: Peripheral to the HRM/TRM line: a biologically inspired latent-iteration model with a fixed tick budget, full backprop through ticks (loss at argmin-loss and argmax-certainty ticks, a form of deep supervision over ticks) and emergent certainty-based halting. Cited by HRM 2506.21734 as related work. Its maze task differs from Maze-Hard (sequence-of-actions output, no positional encodings, 39x39), so numbers are not comparable to HRM/TRM Maze-Hard. No ARC or Sudoku results in this text.

title: Tiny Recursive Models on ARC-AGI-1: Inductive Biases, Identity Conditioning, and Test-Time Compute
relevance_reason: Critique/reproduction of the public TRM ARC-AGI-1 checkpoint isolating test-time voting, puzzle-ID conditioning and effective recursion depth.
one_sentence: Analyzing the ARC Prize TRM verification checkpoint on ARC-AGI-1, the note shows 1000-augmentation voting adds 10.75 points Pass@1, wrong or blank puzzle IDs give 0%, and step-1 recursion already gets 94% of final accuracy.
key_contributions: Quantifies the contribution of 1000-sample test-time augmentation plus majority vote (40.00% vs 29.25% single canonical pass, Pass@1).
Puzzle-identity ablation: blank or random puzzle IDs collapse accuracy to 0%, so the checkpoint depends on per-task embeddings learned from evaluation-task demonstrations.
Per-recursion-step accuracy shows shallow effective recursion; early-training comparison of canonical vs heavy augmentation; efficiency comparison to a naive Llama 3 8B QLoRA fine-tune.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: Checkpoint trained with heavy augmentation (1000 per demonstration pair); new partial runs for 2,500 of ~778,000 steps on ARC-AGI-1 training set under aug 0 vs aug 1000.
setup.loops_train: Fixed four latent cycles in the checkpoint (original paper's strongest uses six).
setup.loops_test: 1-4 recursion steps, extrapolated to 6.
setup.baselines: Single-pass canonical inference; blank/random puzzle ID; Llama 3 8B QLoRA on canonical data.
setup.benchmarks: ARC-AGI-1 public evaluation set (400 tasks), Pass@1 of the aggregated vote; Pass@1000 diagnostic.

title: C-voting: Confidence-Based Test-Time Voting without Explicit Energy Functions
relevance_reason: Test-time scaling by sampling random initial latent states of weight-tied recurrent reasoners (HRM, AKOrN, ItrSA++) and selecting the most confident trajectory.
one_sentence: C-voting samples K random initial latent states, runs the weight-tied recurrence, and picks the candidate with highest mean top-1 probability; with a ~3M attention-only recurrent model (ItrSA++) it reports 95.2% Sudoku-Extreme and 78.6% Maze-Hard versus HRM's 55.0%/74.5%.
key_contributions: C-voting: energy-free, model-agnostic selection among randomly initialized latent trajectories by average top-1 confidence; beats AKOrN's energy-based voting on Sudoku-hard.
ItrSA++: ~3M-parameter recurrent block (cross-attention to input, S self-attention layers, SwiGLU, RMSNorm) with random Gaussian initial state, trained with truncated gradients.
HRM retrofitted with per-input random initial states plus C-voting gives limited gains; calibration analysis explains weak Maze gains (confidently wrong candidates).

setup.model_sizes: ItrSA++ ~3M; AKOrN ~3M; HRM ~27M.
setup.train_tokens_or_data: Sudoku (9,000 train boards), Sudoku-hard used for test; Sudoku-extreme 1,000 train / 1,000 test with HRM's augmentation; Maze-hard 1,000 train / 1,000 test.
setup.loops_train: ItrSA++ T=32 (Sudoku) / T=64 (Maze) blocks; gradient detached at t=2 (Sudoku), t=14 (Sudoku-extreme), t=28 (Maze).
setup.loops_test: Same T; K random initial states (up to 4096 for Sudoku-hard).
setup.baselines: HRM (numbers copied from 2506.21734 for Sudoku-extreme and Maze-hard; rerun for Sudoku-hard), AKOrN with E-voting.
setup.benchmarks: Sudoku-hard, Sudoku-extreme, Maze-hard (board accuracy).

claims.claim: C-voting with 4096 samples on AKOrN reaches 94.4% on Sudoku-hard, 4.9 points above E-voting on the same pretrained model setting.
claims.evidence_quote: The board accuracy in C-voting with 4096 samples is 94.4 ± 0.1%, which is 4.9% higher than that of E-voting (89.5 ± 2.5%) reported in (Miyato et al., 2025).

claims.claim: ItrSA++ with C-voting outperforms HRM on Sudoku-extreme and Maze-hard with about one ninth of HRM's parameters; HRM numbers are taken from the HRM paper (single pass) whereas ItrSA++ uses many sampled trajectories.
claims.regime: unmatched (different parameter counts; HRM single-pass vs ItrSA++ multi-candidate test-time compute)
claims.evidence_quote: It outperforms HRM on Sudoku-extreme (95.2% vs. 55.0%) and Maze-hard tasks (78.6% vs. 74.5%), and AKOrN on Sudoku-hard task (94.4% vs. 89.5%) as shown in Figure 1(b).

claims.claim: Even without voting, ItrSA++ outperforms AKOrN and HRM on all tasks.
claims.evidence_quote: Even without the voting, ItrSA++ outperforms AKOrN and HRM for all the tasks.

claims.claim: C-voting gives limited gains on HRM because HRM is designed around a fixed initial state; ACT was disabled to integrate it.
claims.evidence_quote: Thus, while C-voting shows clear improvements for AKOrN and ItrSA++, its effect on HRM is limited under this modified setting.

venue: Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2026
survey_notes: Test-time scaling via parallel random-init trajectories plus confidence selection, an alternative to TRM-style TTA voting (augmentation-based) and to PTRM (2605.19943, noise injection + Q-head selection) and Speed-is-Confidence (2601.19085, halt-first). Comparison to HRM is unmatched: HRM numbers are single-pass, ItrSA++ uses many candidates, and parameter counts differ. Note ItrSA++ is a single-module, attention-only recurrence with truncated BPTT: further evidence that HRM's two-module hierarchy is not needed for Sudoku-extreme (consistent with 2609.39967, TRM). Cites an ARC Prize team analysis that the two-fold hierarchy had limited effect.

title: Speed is Confidence
relevance_reason: Uses TRM's ACT halting time as a confidence signal for ensembles and trains a single TRM with K parallel latent states via winner-take-all.
one_sentence: For TRM ensembles on Sudoku-Extreme, selecting the first member to halt beats probability averaging (97.2% vs 91.5%) with 10x fewer steps, and winner-take-all training over K=4 latent zL states reaches 96.9% at single-model inference cost.
key_contributions: Halt-first ensembling: run members in parallel, take the answer of the first whose ACT halting logit fires.
Oracle-first (winner-take-all) training: K parallel zL initializations sharing zH, gradient only through the lowest-loss head; internalizes ensemble diversity.

Diagnostic that most baseline failures are selection problems (solvable under another digit permutation); Muon-compatible SwiGLU (RMSNorm before down-projection) enabling 48-minute training on one RTX 5090.

title: Form Follows Function: Recursive Stem Model
relevance_reason: TRM-style shared-weight two-state recursion trained with detached warm-up steps, terminal-only loss and depth curricula; large test-time depth extrapolation on Sudoku/Maze.
one_sentence: RSM keeps the TRM backbone but drops deep supervision: hidden history is detached, loss is applied only at the final outer step, H and L depths grow by curriculum with stochastic two-step gradients, yielding 97.5% Sudoku-Extreme with up to ~20,000 test-time outer steps.
key_contributions: Training contract: detached warm-up iterations, terminal-only loss, optional stochastic inclusion of the penultimate outer step in the gradient (p_detach ~0.99 for Sudoku).
Independent milestone curricula growing outer depth H and inner depth L, with LR re-warmup and stochastic outer-transition to avoid loss spikes.
Test-time depth far beyond training (~20,000 vs ~20 outer steps) and convergence/settling as a reliability signal.

title: When Recursive Models Finish Computing
relevance_reason: Dynamical-systems analysis of TRM checkpoints run far past their nominal recursion budget on hard Sudoku, plus Maze-Hard evaluation-metric audit.
one_sentence: Extending public TRM checkpoints from 16 to 512 outer steps on 1,000 hardest Sudoku-Extreme test puzzles raises exact solves from 59.2% to 87.5% (attention) and 74.4% to 91.9% (MLP); completion coincides with trajectory-aligned contraction despite expanding Jacobian directions.
key_contributions: Shows that >2/3 of nominal-budget failures on hard Sudoku are unfinished computations solved by continuing the same recurrence.

Characterizes completion as trajectory-conditioned anisotropic stability: natural-direction Jacobian gain <1 while the spectral norm stays >1; perturbation experiments; differences between attention and MLP TRMs.
Maze-Hard audit: exact-match understates accuracy because many non-matching outputs are valid paths; constraint-aware top-k decoding recovers Sudoku puzzles.

title: Thinking with Looped Flows
relevance_reason: Trains TRM-architecture looped recurrence with local, temporally aligned flow-matching denoising objectives; best reported single-trajectory ARC-AGI-1/2 among looped models in its table.
one_sentence: Looped flows make the looped model a stateful denoiser trained with per-step denoising losses at decreasing noise levels with shared noise and stop-gradient between steps; inference integrates the probability flow, scaling with finer grids, reaching 58.8% ARC-AGI-1 and 12.2% ARC-AGI-2 pass@2.
key_contributions: Training: sequence of k=16 local denoising objectives on interpolants with sorted decreasing noise levels and shared noise per example; stop-gradient between recurrent steps; ACT head to ignore saturated steps.

Inference: integrate the learned probability flow coupled to the recurrent state (ODE or noise-backtracking SDE); more steps via finer temporal grid; multiple valid solutions from different noise; best-Q ensembling.
Same TRM architecture improves TRM on Sudoku-Extreme, Maze-Hard, ARC-AGI-1/2; resolves 90.9% of TRM's Sudoku failures (non-convergence and spurious attractors); ablations of each flow component.

title: Reasoning on the Simplex: Geometric Fixed-Point Models
relevance_reason: Weight-tied damped Picard iteration where the state is the categorical prediction on a product of simplices; puzzle results vs HRM/TRM/FPRM/EqR plus a 201M looped LM.
one_sentence: GFPR iterates a damped weight-tied Transformer map whose state is a per-site softmax belief (so a fixed point always exists), trains on a differentiated tail after a no-grad rollout, and reports 95.1% Sudoku-Extreme, 92.0% Maze-Hard and a 201M FineWeb-Edu LM.
key_contributions: Belief-state recurrence: state is a field of categorical distributions (plus auxiliary registers) with clues pinned; Brouwer guarantees a fixed point; argmax readable at every step; residual is a stopping rule.

Task-specific convex relaxations (Sudoku consistency polytope, maze unit-flow polytope, doubly stochastic matrices for S5) as structured readouts or recurrent states; unit-flow raises Maze-Hard to 96.0%.
Shows FPRM's halted states on its public Sudoku checkpoint are not fixed points; trains a 201M simplex LM (6B FineWeb-Edu tokens, 24 Picard steps) compared with GPT-2.

title: Symbol-Equivariant Recurrent Reasoning Models
relevance_reason: Symbol-permutation-equivariant variant of HRM/TRM-style recurrent reasoners with deep supervision; reruns HRM/TRM on Sudoku and tests size extrapolation and ARC.

claims.evidence_quote: Addition remains more difficult and separates these two models (80% vs. 66%). The autoregressive TRM performs poorly on all three tasks, reaching only 12%, 11%, and 10% accuracy, respectively.

claims.claim: Single-stream recurrent variants collapse at late output positions on addition, while Dual UT stays stable; only Dense and Dual UT overcome the last-character bottleneck.
claims.evidence_quote: Only Dense and Dual UT reliably break through the final-character bottleneck, with lastcharacter accuracy rising sharply and reaching high values by the end of training.

limitations: Tiny models, small data, three character-level tasks only; authors note results could change at larger scale; TRM adapted with causal mask and no cross-call carry, which removes features of the original TRM.
venue: Published at ICLR 2026 Workshop on AI with Recursive Self-Improvement.
survey_notes: Negative evidence for bringing TRM-style nested refinement to autoregressive LM: under iso-block-evaluation compute, nesting hurts; untied depth wins over tied UT on addition (80 vs 66). Contrasts with HRM-Text (2605.20613), which reports HRM beating FLOP-matched Transformers at 1B on instruction data, but HRM-Text uses PrefixLM, separate H/L weights and truncated BPTT, and matches training FLOPs rather than block passes per token; these differences, not just scale, may explain the disagreement. Also contrasts with HRM-LM 2604.14442 (hierarchy helps vs flat UT).

title: BDH-CQ: In-Context Learning with Recurrent Latent Reasoning
relevance_reason: Recurrent latent reasoning over depth (H_{r+1}=F(H_r,S)) with in-context recurrent memory on ARC-AGI-1; architecture details proprietary.
one_sentence: BDH-CQ (150M, Dragon Hatchling family) ingests ARC demonstrations into a recurrent memory and iterates a latent workspace to answer the query, reaching 29.5% pass@2 on public ARC-AGI-1 at $0.0007 per task without task IDs or evaluation demonstrations in training.
key_contributions: Inductive (non-transductive) ARC protocol for a latent recurrent reasoner: no task identifiers, no evaluation-task demonstration pairs in training, no test-time parameter updates.
Cost-accuracy operating point: 29.5% pass@2 at about 0.85 H200 GPU-seconds per task, independently reproduced by a black-box audit.
ConceptARC concept-family capability profile and controlled ARC-like interventions on binding and extrapolation.

setup.loops_test: Not disclosed.

claims.evidence_quote: At the default point, the 150M-parameter system reaches 29.5% pass@2 in approximately 0.85 H200 GPU-seconds per task. At $3 per H200-hour this gives a computed cost of $0.00070 per task

claims.claim: Unlike HRM/TRM ARC pipelines, neither task identifiers nor evaluation-task demonstrations are used in training.
claims.evidence_quote: Neither task identifiers nor evaluation-task demonstration pairs participate in training, and no parameters are updated at inference time.

Proprietary details prevent verifying recurrence structure; treat as adjacent.

title: Self-Supervised Transformers as Iterative Solution Improvers for Constraint Satisfaction
relevance_reason: A Transformer trained (self-supervised) for one refinement step and applied iteratively at test time on CSPs; test-time iteration as depth, but no latent recurrence across steps.
one_sentence: ConsFormer trains a Transformer with differentiable constraint penalties to improve a random CSP assignment in one step, then iterates it thousands of times at test time, solving 77.74% of out-of-distribution hard Sudokus at 10k iterations.
key_contributions: Self-supervised training with continuous relaxations of discrete constraints, no feasible-solution labels.
Single-step training, iterative deployment: more test-time iterations solve harder OOD instances.
Results on Sudoku, Graph Coloring, Nurse Rostering and MAXCUT.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: 9K training instances per problem (SATNet Sudoku in-distribution; RRN test set as harder OOD).
setup.loops_train: Single refinement step.
setup.loops_test: Up to 2k-10k iterations.
setup.baselines: Learned CSP solvers including Yang et al. (2023) recurrent Transformer, ANYCSP; OR-Tools.
setup.benchmarks: Sudoku (in-distribution and OOD), Graph Coloring, Nurse Rostering, MAXCUT.

claims.claim: Iterating a one-step-trained refiner at test time solves out-of-distribution hard Sudoku, improving with more iterations (65.88% at 2k, 77.74% at 10k).
claims.regime: unmatched (vs published learned solvers); iso_param across iteration counts
claims.evidence_quote: ConsFormer achieves instance solve rates of 65.88% and 77.74% with 2k and 10k iterations, respectively.

claims.claim: Authors attribute better test-time scaling than a 32-iteration-trained recurrent Transformer to training for a single iteration.
claims.evidence_quote: This could be due to Yang et al. (2023)'s approach being trained for 32 iterations, while ConsFormer was trained for a single iteration, allowing it to generalize better when applied iteratively.

limitations: Sudoku benchmarks are SATNet/RRN sets, not Sudoku-Extreme; no hidden state carried across iterations (state is the assignment).
venue: Proceedings of the 42 nd International Conference on Machine Learning, Vancouver, Canada. PMLR 267, 2025.
builds_on: Yang et al. 2023 (looped Transformer on Sudoku)
survey_notes: Predecessor-style evidence that iterating a prediction-space refinement map scales with test-time compute; conceptually close to GFPR (2609.33540, state is the prediction) and RSM (2603.15641, depth-agnostic operator trained shallow). Not comparable to Sudoku-Extreme numbers.

title: G-RRM: Guiding Symbolic Solvers with Recurrent Reasoning Models
relevance_reason: Uses SE-RRM recurrent reasoning models as neural hint generators for backtracking/SAT solvers; application of looped reasoners rather than a new looped method.
one_sentence: G-RRM feeds SE-RRM full-assignment proposals as branching hints to backtracking and SAT solvers; on 9x9 Sudoku (SE-RRM 91.1% correct) backtracking speeds up 33.3x and Glucose 1.70x, while CaDiCaL, which cannot overwrite hints, gains nothing.
key_contributions: Neuro-symbolic pipeline: recurrent reasoning model proposals guide classical CSP/SAT solvers to guaranteed-correct solutions.
Identifies two conditions for speedups: large combinatorial search space and solvers that can overwrite imperfect hints.

setup.baselines: Unguided backtracking, Glucose 4.1, CaDiCaL 3.0.0.
setup.benchmarks: Sudoku 9x9 to 25x25 solver runtime and conflicts.

claims.claim: Neural guidance from SE-RRM yields large speedups for backtracking and Glucose on 9x9 Sudoku, but not for CaDiCaL whose runtime is overhead-dominated and which always respects hints.
claims.evidence_quote: on 9 × 9 Sudoku, where the SE-RRM correctly solves 91.1% of instances, backtracking accelerates by 33.3× and Glucose 4.1 by 1.70× (median, p < 0.001)

limitations: Read at abstract level only (priority 3).
survey_notes: Shows one practical use of recursive reasoners: correctness via symbolic verification/search, addressing the no-guarantee failure mode. Its 91.1% SE-RRM figure on 9x9 Sudoku differs from 93.73% (16 steps) in 2603.02193, likely different instances or settings; protocol not checked.

title: CosmicFish-HRM: Adaptive Reasoning via Hierarchical Recurrent Mechanisms in Compact Language Models
relevance_reason: Compact autoregressive LM with an HRM core iterating H/L cycles and a Q-style learned halting head.
one_sentence: An 82.77M LM with an HRM reasoning core and learned halting trained on 10B tokens allocates non-uniform reasoning steps but does not beat similar-size Transformers (GPT-2 Small, OPT-125M, Pythia-160M) on zero-shot HellaSwag/PIQA/WinoGrande.
key_contributions: HRM-style H/L recurrent core inside a GQA/RoPE/SwiGLU decoder with halt/continue head, exploration during training and inference halt bias.
Analysis of reasoning-step allocation across tasks and inputs.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: CosmicSet, 10B tokens (web, Wikipedia, code, math, papers).
setup.loops_train: H/L cycles up to a maximum number of reasoning steps with learned halting.
setup.loops_test: Learned halting with bias delta=0.35 toward early stopping.
setup.baselines: CosmicFish-90M/120M without HRM core; GPT-2 Small, OPT-125M, Pythia-160M.
setup.benchmarks: HellaSwag, PIQA, WinoGrande, TriviaQA, ARC-Easy, Natural Questions (zero-shot).

claims.claim: At compact scale the HRM core does not improve zero-shot accuracy over similar-size Transformers; authors hypothesize the overhead amortizes at larger scale (untested).
claims.regime: unmatched (different data; non-HRM CosmicFish variants differ in size)
claims.evidence_quote: At compact scale, CosmicFish-HRM does not outperform conventional transformers of similar size on these benchmarks.

numbers.what: Zero-shot HellaSwag/PIQA/WinoGrande: CosmicFish-HRM

limitations: Small scale, shallow benchmarks not designed for iterative reasoning; no matched non-recurrent control at the same size and data; scaling hypothesis untested.
survey_notes: Negative/neutral LM data point for HRM-style recurrence at <100M scale; contrasts with HRM-Text (1B, instruction data, strong gains) and is consistent with AR-TRM (2603.08082) finding no benefit for TRM-style nesting in small autoregressive models. Low evidential weight (single author, no controlled baseline).

title: Latent Recurrent Thoughts: Recurrent Refinement of Proposed Latents for Reasoning with Frozen LLMs
relevance_reason: Uses TRM's recursive module as a small recurrent refiner of latent thought vectors fed to a frozen Qwen3-8B; recursion lives in an auxiliary module, not the LM.
one_sentence: LRT trains a ~4.2M proposer and a ~7M TRM-style recurrent refiner to produce continuous latent thoughts for a frozen Qwen3-8B, beating frozen-decoder latent-reasoning baselines on Countdown-4, Sudoku, HumanEval, MBPP and StrategyQA at matched budget.
key_contributions: Frozen-LLM latent reasoning where the latents come from a tiny recurrent refiner (TRM recursion with input re-injection and bounded residual corrections).
Controlled comparison with identical frozen decoder, prompts, data and budget; refiner scaling 7M -> 28M improves Countdown-4 and HumanEval monotonically.

setup.model_sizes: Frozen Qwen3-8B; trainable ~11.2M (proposer ~4.2M, refiner ~7M; refiner scaled to 28M).
setup.train_tokens_or_data: Task answer supervision without reasoning traces.
setup.loops_train: Truncated-gradient unrolling following TRM.
setup.baselines: Direct, Zero-shot CoT, prior frozen-decoder continuous-space methods (e.g. EBM-CoT), prefix/P-tuning; reference: thinking mode, MGDM, TRM, EqR.
setup.benchmarks: Countdown-4, Sudoku, HumanEval, MBPP, StrategyQA.

claims.claim: Scaling only the recurrent refiner (7M to 28M) with the decoder frozen improves Countdown-4 from 56.7 to 69.1 and HumanEval from 37.8 to 46.1.
claims.evidence_quote: Countdown-4 rises from 56.7 to 66.3 to 69.1, and HumanEval from 37.8 to 44.0 to 46.1.

claims.claim: On Sudoku, thinking-mode Qwen3-8B fails (0.5) while the 7M refiner reaches 49.2; from-scratch symbolic solvers (TRM, EqR) remain far higher.
claims.evidence_quote: Sudoku, is exactly where it fails (0.5) while a 7M recurrent refiner reaches 49.2: token-space search is not a substitute for iterative computation on a constraint-satisfaction substrate.

limitations: Abstract-plus-scan reading (priority 3); Sudoku dataset may differ from Sudoku-Extreme (TRM listed at 97.2 in its reference table, vs 87.4 on Sudoku-Extreme in TRM's paper).
survey_notes: Hybrid: TRM-style recursion as a plug-in reasoning module for a frozen LLM, one route to bring recursive reasoners to language other than pretraining an HRM LM (HRM-Text, Mimir) or editing explicit candidates (R-Qwen 2608.01534).

title: Parameter-Efficient Quality Estimation via Frozen Recursive Models
relevance_reason: Applies TRM's shared-network recursion (internal L cycles, external refinement steps) to MT quality estimation on frozen embeddings.
one_sentence: On low-resource MT quality estimation for 8 language pairs, TRM's external iteration hurts and internal recursion helps only narrowly; a 7M TRM head on frozen XLM-R embeddings reaches Spearman 0.370, above an equal-depth standard Transformer (0.336).
key_contributions: Three-phase test of TRM mechanisms on a regression task (QE): external iteration steps 1-16 and L cycles 1-6.
Frozen pretrained embeddings match fine-tuned ones with 37x fewer trainable parameters.

setup.model_sizes: TRM-QE 7M trainable on frozen XLM-R (vs 262M fine-tuned).
setup.train_tokens_or_data: Low-resource QE dataset, 8 language pairs.
setup.loops_train: External iteration 1-16 steps, Lcycles 1-6 (ablation).
setup.baselines: Fine-tuned variants, equivalent-depth standard Transformer, MonoTransQuest (560M).
setup.benchmarks: Spearman/Pearson correlation for QE.

claims.claim: TRM's recursive mechanisms do not transfer to QE: single-step models are best on external iteration, and internal recursion gives only narrow benefits.
claims.evidence_quote: Contrary to intuitions from reasoning tasks, single-step models achieve the highest correlation (0.333 Pearson, 0.324 Spearman),

claims.claim: Frozen-embedding TRM-QE (0.370 Spearman) outperforms an equivalent-depth standard Transformer (0.336).
claims.evidence_quote: TRM-QE with frozen XLM-R embeddings achieves a Spearman's correlation of 0.370, matching fine-tuned variants (0.369) and outperforming an equivalentdepth standard transformer (0.336).

limitations: Abstract-plus-scan reading (priority 3); single regression task family.
survey_notes: Out-of-domain negative result: TRM's outer-loop refinement (deep supervision steps) does not help a non-search regression task; supports the view that recursive-reasoner gains are task-dependent (search/constraint tasks), cf. 2609.39967's domain-dependent test-time gains.

title: Selection, Reflection and Self-Refinement: Revisit Reasoning Tasks via a Causal Lens
relevance_reason: Single shared Transformer layer unrolled as a fixed-point latent refiner with input/feedback injection and periodic intermediate alignment; compared to HRM and recurrent-depth baselines on Sudoku-Extreme, Maze-Hard, ARC.
one_sentence: SR2 casts reasoning as selection over dense latent dependencies and implements reflective representation learning, dependency self-refinement with a single recurrent Transformer layer, and periodic intermediate alignment, reaching 66.63% Sudoku-Extreme and 93.7% Maze-Hard at 3.4M parameters.
key_contributions: Causal 'selection mechanism' view of reasoning tasks motivating latent feedback (reflection) and dependency self-refinement.
Flattened recurrent Transformer: one shared block unrolled as fixed-point iteration, with feedback injection and periodic intermediate supervision.
Comparison ladder on Sudoku-Extreme/Maze-Hard: Transformer, Block Universal Transformer, Recurrent Depth (input injection), Reflective Model, HRM, SR2.

setup.model_sizes: SR2 3.4M (single Transformer layer backbone); Transformer/HRM/Reflective 27.3M (8 layers).
setup.train_tokens_or_data: Sudoku-Extreme and Maze-Hard following HRM configuration.
setup.loops_train: Unrolled fixed number of refinement steps with periodic intermediate alignment every M steps.
setup.baselines: Transformer, Block Universal Transformer, Recurrent Depth, Reflective Model, HRM (same optimizer, lr, batch).
setup.benchmarks: Sudoku-Extreme, Maze-Hard, ARC-1, ARC-2 (pass@1).

claims.claim: SR2 beats HRM by 11.6 points on Sudoku-Extreme and 19.2 on Maze-Hard with one eighth of the parameters.
claims.regime: iso_data, unmatched in parameters (3.4M vs 27.3M); HRM numbers equal HRM's published values
claims.evidence_quote: Moreover, SR2 surpasses HRM by 11.6% on Sudoku-Extreme and 19.2% on Maze-Hard, while using only one eighth of HRM's parameters.

claims.claim: A non-hierarchical Reflective Model matches HRM at equal parameters, suggesting the hierarchy is not necessary; input injection is what lifts a flat shared block (Block UT) to Recurrent Depth.
claims.evidence_quote: HRM achieves results comparable to the Reflective Model, suggesting that hierarchical recurrent structures are not strictly necessary for reasoning tasks of this type.

venue: Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2026
survey_notes: Another independent result that hierarchy is unnecessary (Reflective Model ~ HRM), and that input injection is critical for flat weight-tied recurrence (Block UT 0% Sudoku vs Recurrent Depth 42.52%), in line with 2609.39967; relevant to interpreting the flat-UniTF failure in 2604.14442. Maze-Hard 93.7% is the highest single-model Maze number in this group, above TRM 85.3, FPRM 87.0, GFPR 92.0.

title: What Limits Recursive Reasoning Models: Optimization, Architecture and Test-Time Scaling
relevance_reason: Controlled re-implementation and one-factor-at-a-time ablation of HRM/TRM/URM recursive reasoners across six domains; identifies which components matter.
one_sentence: Retraining HRM, TRM and URM in one codebase across six domains, the paper finds an intermediate gradient horizon, large physical batches and bounded/gated state updates matter most, explicit H/L separation does not, and builds a 13.6M model beating all three.
key_contributions: Unified pipeline re-training HRM, TRM, URM with matched data representation, tokenization and evaluation on Sudoku, Maze, ARC-AGI-1/2, plus new Game of Life and Arithmetic tasks with controlled OOD splits.

Controlled ablations: gradient horizon (KL,KH) has an interior optimum; physical batch beats gradient accumulation at equal effective batch; shared vs separate H/L modules at matched parameters shows no consistent winner; cumulative stabilization (gate, clipping, consistent dropout, relative noise) mainly cuts seed variance.

A 13.6M shared-block recipe with (H,L)=(4,2) cycles, gradients through last (2,2) cycles, bounded+gated+normalized updates; reports compute accounting showing parameter sharing does not reduce sequential compute.

setup.model_sizes: Ours 13.6M (one shared 4-layer post-norm block, hidden 512); HRM 27M (4+4 layers), TRM 7M (2 layers), URM 7M (2-layer config) as retrained baselines; 8-layer dense control.
setup.train_tokens_or_data: Sudoku-Extreme full training split without symmetry augmentation; Maze-30x30-hard; ARC-AGI-1 combined with ConceptARC (transductive, 1000 augmentations per puzzle); ARC-AGI-2 separate; 200k Game of Life trajectories; RPN arithmetic split by operand multiset.
setup.loops_train: (Hcycles,Lcycles)=(4,2) per ACT step; ACT budget max 16 steps (8 for ARC-AGI-1) with detached carry; gradients through final (KH,KL)=(2,2) cycles.
setup.loops_test: Halting disabled, full ACT budget executed; test-time scaling by extending ACT budget.
setup.baselines: HRM, TRM, URM retrained in same codebase; dense non-recurrent control; Qwen3-30B-A3B and Qwen3.6-27B from released checkpoints without fine-tuning.
setup.benchmarks: Arithmetic ID/OOD, Game of Life ID/OOD, Maze, Sudoku (exact accuracy); ARC-AGI-1/2 pass@1 and pass@2 with augmentation voting.

claims.claim: Explicit hierarchy (separate H/L parameters) is not a universal source of improvement: at matched parameter count shared modules win on Maze and ARC-AGI-1, separate ones give small gains on Sudoku and Game of Life.
claims.evidence_quote: Shared modules perform better on Maze and ARC-AGI-1, while separate modules provide small gains on Sudoku and Game of Life; the two configurations are nearly identical on Arithmetic.

claims.claim: Gradient horizon through the nested recurrence has an interior optimum: (KL,KH)=(2,2) gives the best Arithmetic OOD accuracy while (1,3), with the same number of differentiated applications, overfits ID.
claims.evidence_quote: The intermediate setting (KL , KH ) = (2, 2) achieves the highest OOD accuracy of 71.16%, whereas (1, 3) reaches the highest ID accuracy of 99.60% but generalizes poorly, obtaining only 17.88% OOD.

claims.claim: Gradient accumulation does not reproduce a large physical batch for recursive models: at fixed effective batch 8192, Game of Life OOD drops sharply with accumulation.
claims.evidence_quote: OOD accuracy decreases from 63.16% with a physical batch of 8192 to 37.71% with four accumulation steps, while the mean pre-clipping gradient norm increases from 0.38 to 65.46.

claims.claim: Larger recurrent blocks and extra test-time ACT steps give only domain-dependent gains (largest on Arithmetic and Sudoku, limited on Game of Life, Maze, ARC).
claims.evidence_quote: Increasing the recurrent block from four to eight layers, increasing hidden size, or adding attention heads does not yield consistent accuracy gains across the tested settings.

claims.claim: On ARC-AGI-1 the non-recurrent dense control is already competitive with recursive models; recursion helps most on Sudoku and Maze.
claims.evidence_quote: ARC behaves differently: on ARC-AGI-1 the dense control is already competitive, while all systems remain limited on ARC-AGI-2.

claims.claim: Parameter sharing reduces parameter count but not sequential inference cost: TRM and the 13.6M model have similar recurrent compute per answer.
claims.evidence_quote: Parameter sharing therefore primarily reduces parameter count rather than sequential computation: TRM and our configuration have substantially different parameter counts but similar recurrent inference cost.

title: Probabilistic Tiny Recursive Model
relevance_reason: Inference-only test-time scaling for TRM via noisy parallel latent rollouts and Q-head selection; reports Sudoku-Extreme, Maze-Hard, ARC-AGI-2 and PPBench.
one_sentence: PTRM adds Gaussian noise to TRM's latent at every deep-recursion (supervision) step, runs K parallel rollouts and picks the answer with the highest Q-head value, lifting a pretrained TRM from 87.3% to 98.75% on Sudoku-Extreme without retraining.
key_contributions: Diagnosis: TRM failures are trajectories trapped in bad latent basins; the halting Q head tracks cell accuracy and separates correct from incorrect trajectories.
Width scaling: K noisy rollouts plus best-Q selection; pass@K vs best-Q@K gap under 1pp on PPBench validation; width gains exceed depth gains.
Results on PPBench golden set (62.6% to 91.2%), Sudoku-Extreme (to 98.75%), Maze-Hard (to 86.73% with mode@K), ARC-AGI-2 (pass@1 7.36% to 8.47%), and cost comparison to frontier LLMs.

setup.model_sizes: TRM-MLP 5M (Sudoku-Extreme), TRM-Att 7M (Maze-Hard, ARC-AGI-2, PPBench); direct-prediction baseline 27M.
setup.train_tokens_or_data: Standard TRM checkpoints and splits for Sudoku-Extreme, Maze-Hard, ARC-AGI-2; PPBench training set with 10x augmentation (trajectory sampling + dihedral).
setup.loops_train: Standard TRM: n latent updates then one answer update per latent recursion, T recursions per deep-recursion step (only last with gradient), up to Nsup=16 supervision steps.
setup.loops_test: D supervision steps (16-64) x K rollouts (25-100); e.g. Sudoku-Extreme K=100, D=64, sigma=0.3.
setup.baselines: Deterministic TRM (same checkpoint), published HRM/TRM/direct-pred numbers, frontier LLMs on PPBench (direct, agentic, oracle ensemble).
setup.benchmarks: PPBench golden set (sudoku, lightup, nurikabe, heyawake, tapa), Sudoku-Extreme, Maze-Hard, ARC-AGI-2 (pass@1/2/100 with augmentation voting).

claims.claim: On Sudoku-Extreme, noisy rollouts with Q-head selection lift the deterministic TRM checkpoint from 87.3% to 98.75% (best-Q@K), using K=100 rollouts and 64 supervision steps.
claims.regime: iso_param (same checkpoint; inference compute ~100x and 4x depth)
claims.evidence_quote: On Sudoku-Extreme, PTRM at K=100, D=64, σ=0.3 raises the deterministic baseline of 87.3% to 99.06% pass@K and 98.75% best-Q@K, achieving state of the art.

claims.claim: On Maze-Hard noise unlocks many correct rollouts (pass@K 95.63%) but the Q head selects them poorly (best-Q@K 85.17%, mode@K 86.73%).
claims.evidence_quote: On Maze-Hard, PTRM at K=100, D=16, σ=1.0 reaches 95.63% pass@K, an 11.83 point gain over the 83.8% deterministic baseline. mode@K gives the best PTRM accuracy here at 86.73%

claims.claim: On ARC-AGI-2, PTRM gives a small pass@1 gain and no pass@2 gain over deterministic TRM with augmentation voting.
claims.evidence_quote: With K=25 and σ=0.2, PTRM lifts pass@1 from 7.36% to 8.47% and pass@100 from 14.31% to 15.97% over our deterministic TRM baseline, while matching it at pass@2.

claims.claim: Width scaling dominates depth scaling: tripling depth at K=1 adds 3.1pp on PPBench validation while K=100 adds about 13pp.
claims.evidence_quote: On the deterministic baseline (K=1), tripling the depth from 16 to 48 steps raises PPBench validation accuracy from 76.4% to 79.5% (+3.1pp).

claims.claim: Against frontier LLMs on the PPBench golden set, PTRM (91.2%) beats the strongest direct-strategy LLM and an oracle ensemble of 7 LLMs; this is an unmatched comparison (task-trained 7M model vs general LLMs).
claims.evidence_quote: PTRM exceeds the strongest single LLM (direct strategy) by 57 points aggregate (91.2% vs. 34.7%), and exceeds the LLM ensemble by 36 points (91.2% vs. 55.1%)

numbers.what: TRM template as described by PTRM (co-authored by TRM's author): inner latent updates then answer update with one two-layer network
numbers.value: n z-updates + 1 y-update per latent recursion
numbers.quote: a single latent recursion consists of n updates to the latent state z followed by one update to the predicted answer y, all using the same two-layer network

numbers.what: TRM gradient: only the last of T latent recursions keeps gradients; deep supervision up to Nsup steps
numbers.quote: A deep recursion runs T latent recursions in sequence, with only the final one retaining gradients, allowing the model to leverage a large effective depth while keeping training efficient.

numbers.what: TRM inference does not use the Q head; runs all Nsup steps
numbers.quote: During inference, the Q head is not used, and the model performs Nsup supervision steps to maximize answer correctness.

limitations: Puzzle tasks only, small grids, PPBench subset; gains small on ARC-AGI-2 and Heyawake; Q head is a weak verifier on Maze-Hard; inference compute scales with K x D. Conclusion states 'ARC-AGI (from 7.8% to 8.47% pass@1)' although 7.8% is TRM's published pass@2 (Table 3) and the reproduced pass@1 baseline is 7.36%.
builds_on: Ren and Liu 2601.10679 (spurious fixed points in HRM)
Efstathiou and Balwani (noise on initial z)
survey_notes: Width-axis test-time scaling for recursive reasoners; co-authored by the TRM author. Compare with C-voting (2604.13521: random initial state + confidence selection), Speed-is-Confidence (2601.19085: halt-first selection), GFPR (2609.33540). Protocol: Sudoku-Extreme 98.75% uses 100 rollouts x 64 steps on the 1000-example-trained TRM-MLP checkpoint, so it is iso-param but ~400x the default inference compute; contrast 2609.39967's 98.41% which uses the full Sudoku training split. The ARC-AGI-2 pass@1 vs pass@2 mix-up in the conclusion is a precise inconsistency to flag. Reports Q-head-as-verifier works on Sudoku/PPBench but not Maze.
